newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Security main worry for Kuwaitis in Monday poll.
newsitem.headline: Security main worry for Kuwaitis in Monday poll.

text.p: Security, the economy and jobs are key issues dominating rallies ahead of Monday's election of a parliament that will take Kuwait into the next century.

SECURITY - Concern over the security of the tiny state tops the list of priorities despite the presence of American military forces in Kuwait and the region since a U.S.-led coalition freed Kuwait from a seven-month Iraqi occupation in 1991. Officials and politicians say Baghdad will be a threat to the oil-rich region as long as Iraq's Saddam Hussein remained in power. Critics, including Parliament Speaker Ahmad al-Saadoun, say the government had failed to move fast enough to build a deterrent Kuwaiti force. Alleged fraud in Defence Ministry contracts -- firmly denied by the government -- are also adding to the unease of Kuwaitis.

ECONOMIC REFORMS - Gulf War costs, Iraq's occupation and earlier weak oil prices have all contributed to a drop in Kuwait's foreign reserves to about $35 billion from more than $100 billion six years ago. MPs say alleged fraud and misuse of public funds are also to blame. Voters and candidates are eager to see parliament gain more powers to monitor and curb state spending. But ordinary Kuwaitis are worried about calls by international financial bodies and some politicians for the introduction of income and corporate taxes for Kuwaitis to help balance the budget of the generous welfare state. The outgoing parliament on Tuesday approved a $14 billion 1996/97 budget with a $4 billion deficit.

JOBS - Unless Kuwait boosts state revenue and encourages the private sector to hire more Kuwaitis it will not meet the hopes of a rapidly growing population for jobs which the state is obliged by the constitution to provide. Most Kuwaitis work for the state which also grants them land and soft loans to build a home or pays them a housing allowance. More than a third of the state's revenue of $10 billion is spent on wages.

STATELESS PEOPLE - There are about 120,000 stateless people in the country of about two million, including 700,000 Kuwaitis. They claim to be Kuwaitis who did not acquire proper documents after Kuwait's 1961 independence. Kuwait says most are mainly from regional states seeking to enjoy welfare benefits granted to Kuwaitis. Some politicians and officials see them as a security hazard but say those who fought against Iraq should be granted Kuwaiti nationality. Some of the stateless people serve in the military and police forces.

WOMEN - Kuwaiti women will hold a silent march on election day to demand political rights. They cannot vote or run for parliament although they are over 50 percent of Kuwaitis and regarded as the most liberal women in a Moslem conservative region. Some of the 237 candidates, including leading liberal MPs and Islamists, support the right for women to vote but their 30-year-old campaign has yet to bear fruit.
